new_statements.rule_in_words: The SIL phonology statement for the Kuni dialect denies word-level stress altogether; prominence is a clause-level phenomenon that tracks the grammatical tone melodies (tone distinguishes tense/mood/polarity/clause type on the verb and adjoining phrases, not lexical items). No default stressed syllable in citation forms is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Related remarks: vowel length is grammatically contrastive (verb prefixes); in everyday speech the vowel of the second syllable of a 3+-syllable word before a closed syllable is often dropped (p.8), which hints at reduction of that position but is not framed as stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly word vs clause: no word-level stress; clause-level stress follows the grammatical tone patterns. Source is an 8-page OPD (draft, not peer reviewed) by long-term SIL fieldworkers; describes the Kuni dialect (Glottolog kuni1266) of Kuni-Boazi.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted OPD describes the Kuni dialect (Glottolog kuni1266, villages Boimbalavu, Dimu, Tagum, Usokof, Magipopo, Ogia, Kubut) of Kuni-Boazi kuni1265 [kvg]; Voorhoeve 1970 treats 'Kuini' as one of three Boazi dialects and notes only sub-phonemic differences from Boset (South) Boazi, but the no-word-stress/grammatical-tone claim is attested here only for Kuni.

sources.note: Sec. 5 'Suprasegmentals (tone, intonation, stress)', p.7: 'There is no stress on word level. On clause level, stress follows mainly the tone patterns.' Also: contrastive GRAMMATICAL tone at clause level (30+ patterns, e.g. geteít 'He ran' vs géteít 'He intends to run'), 'No lexical tone contrasts have been found'; vowel length grammatically relevant.

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C.L. 1970. The Languages of the Lake Murray Area. In Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 12, pp. 1-18. Pacific Linguistics A-25. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-A25.1.
sources.note: Sec. 2 Phonology (pp.4-6) gives consonant/vowel inventories and allophony for Boset-Boazi, North Boazi, Kuini, Zimakani, Begua, plus cluster/word-final constraints; nothing on stress or accent. The comparative wordlist 'in phonetic notation' (pp.7-18, page image checked) carries no stress marks.
